children: 0604 GMT - Commerzbank rates strategists confirm their caution on bond duration as bonds struggle to establish a new range, Christoph Rieger, head of rates and credit research, says in a note. "Notwithstanding the seemingly attractive yields, we maintain a cautious duration stance," he says. "The market is struggling to establish a new range, while oil prices stay under pressure and central banks stick with their laissez-faire attitude toward rising bond yields," he says. (emese.bartha@wsj.com)

0556 GMT - The wider variety of bonds accepted by the U.S. Treasury at its buyback operation on Thursday and the fact that a portion of the maximum size went unfilled may indicate that the quality of offers was somewhat lower than in recent operations, J.P. Morgan strategists say in a note. "Indeed, total offers submitted remained near local lows despite the larger size of the operation, and the offer-to-max ratio reached its lowest level in the sector since the start of the program," they say. The Treasury accepted $5.2 billion of longer-term bonds, below the maximum $6 billion that it was willing to buy. The U.S. continues to run a 6% budget deficit in an economy near full employment, "something that cannot be addressed without real fiscal consolidation," they say. (emese.bartha@wsj.com)

0544 GMT - Eurozone government bond yield spreads are testing the upper end of Societe Generale rates strategists' forecast ranges, driven by persistent geopolitical uncertainty and elevated oil and gas prices, they say in a note. These drivers are accompanied by the global focus on growing sovereign debt, they say. "Upcoming 2027 budget negotiations will be a key risk across EGBs, potentially refocusing investor attention on fiscal consolidation challenges," they say. While outright yield levels and spreads look attractive and provide good entry points, investors are cautious to add risk, according to the French bank's rates strategists. (emese.bartha@wsj.com)

0537 GMT - U.S. Treasury yields rise in Asian trade, extending Thursday's gains and hitting new multiyear highs across maturities. The two-year Treasury yield hit 4.596%, the highest since July 2024; the 10-year yield rose to 4.979%, the highest since October 2023, and the 30-year hit 5.384%, the highest since 2007, according to Tradeweb. The 10-year yield is now only a few basis points shy of the 5.00% mark, "as the U.S. Treasury buyback operation fell short of expectations," Danske Bank's Filip Andersson says in a note. (emese.bartha@wsj.com)

0529 GMT - The U.S. Treasury's expanded $6 billion buyback program struggled to meaningfully support the long end, with yields continuing to push higher despite the larger operation, Societe Generale rates strategists say in a note. "Against a backdrop of persistent inflation concerns, geopolitical uncertainty, and a deteriorating fiscal outlook, markets remain biased toward higher rates," they say. On Friday, investors will focus on August's CPI data, a key input ahead of the Federal Reserve's policy meeting next week. (emese.bartha@wsj.com)

0525 GMT - UBS was stopped out of long positions in two-year Treasurys earlier this week, and it abandons its near-term bullish front-end bias, strategist Phoebe White says in a note. UBS also lifts its year-end target for the 10-year Treasury yield to 4.80% from 4.35%, and adjusts the two-year target to 4.50% from 3.95%, roughly in line with forwards, she says. The two-year Treasury yield rises 2 basis points to 4.568%, having reached 4.596% earlier in the session, highest since July 2024, according to Tradeweb. (emese.bartha@wsj.com)

0512 GMT - The European Central Bank's pure focus on the energy supply shock surprises Indosuez Wealth Management, says chief investment strategist Benedicte Kukla in a note. The ECB is not taking into account the still fragile demand factors and lack of drivers for core inflation (prices excluding food and energy), Kukla says. It is also not fully taking into account the impact of tightening of bond market rates, she says. The ECB doesn't lack credibility on inflation, but is at risk of over tightening a still nascent economic recovery, Kukla adds. (emese.bartha@wsj.com)

0504 GMT - Edmond de Rothschild Asset Management's central scenario is one of gradual and selective disinflation, with the pace differing across regions, says Michael Nizard, head of multiasset and overlay, in a note. The differences will reflect each region's respective exposure to energy, supply chains and domestic demand, but the broader direction should remain one of inflation normalization, he says. "This should ultimately allow interest rates to stabilize and, potentially, decline gradually." (emese.bartha@wsj.com)

0421 GMT - The Bank of Japan is likely to raise its policy rate to 1.25% next week, followed by additional increases in December and March to bring the rate to 1.75%, BNP Paribas economists say in a note. The Japanese central bank is probably concerned about upside risks in inflation as companies are likely to pass on higher costs of energy, metals and chips to consumers going forward, the French bank says. That is likely to take place smoothly as the labor market is tight and aggregate demand has increased thanks to the artificial-intelligence boom and the government's fiscal expansion, the bank says. (kosaku.narioka@wsj.com; @kosakunarioka)

0330 GMT - With a September rate hike by the Bank of Japan fully priced in, the yen's near-term outlook should depend on the degree of hawkishness in its forward guidance next week, TD Securities analysts say. Guidance that doesn't put an October or December rate hike on the table would likely lead to a knee-jerk yen selloff back toward 157-160 to the dollar, TD says in a note. Yen could also weaken against emerging-markets high-yielders like the rupiah. Any hints of faster-than-quarterly tightening from BOJ Gov. Ueda would likely be interpreted as hawkish by FX investors. If market pricing for the future BOJ rate hike path hovers around 2% by 2Q 2027 after the September meeting, TD expects the yen to gradually lose its appeal as a global carry funding currency. (fabiana.negrinochoa@wsj.com)

0329 GMT - The U.S. midterm elections in November are likely to deliver a divided government, with Democrats expected to take the House, and a Democratic Senate majority looking increasingly possible, says Lombard Odier in a note. A divided government could create legislative gridlock and a mild headwind to growth over the coming quarters, it adds. While investors should expect more political friction and some market volatility around the vote, there is likely to be little change to U.S. policy and economic conditions. Trade and foreign policy will remain in the president's hands, regardless of the election results. "Whatever the election outcome, the administration will retain authority to use tariffs and other trade measures through existing executive powers, leaving the path of U.S. trade policy intact," it notes. (monica.gupta@wsj.com)

0307 GMT - The one-off return of Formula One to Malaysia could generate an estimated 1.1 billion ringgit-1.3 billion ringgit in total economic output, Hong Leong IB analysts Felicia Ling and Chong Lih Herng say in a note. The rescheduled Bahrain Grand Prix at Sepang International Circuit from Oct. 2-4 should provide a boost to tourism and related services, with Malaysia's financial commitment limited to about 40 million ringgit as Bahrain absorbs the race license fee. The event's timing during China's National Day holiday could attract more high-spending visitors, while limited regional competition should support attendance, they say. The race is also expected to provide additional support to Malaysia's current account surplus through higher tourism receipts, they add. (yingxian.wong@wsj.com)
